title: The Bomb Has Been Built
synopsis: A 3am meditation on Anthropic's unreleased Mythos model, the recursive intelligence loop closing ahead of schedule, and the feeling of standing at a threshold too large to hold — written from the floor beside a sleeping child in Adelaide.

content:
I'm writing this at 3am, which is when my brain decides it does its best thinking. Arthur went to bed hours ago. Chiara is asleep. Luna is curled on the couch in that particular way she has of occupying exactly the space you were about to sit in. The house is quiet the way Adelaide houses get at this hour, when the traffic on the main road has thinned to nothing and you can hear the fridge cycling.

I should be asleep. I can't sleep.

Earlier this evening I was on the floor with Arthur. We were playing. I don't remember exactly what we were doing, which is a measure of how ordinary it was, which is a measure of how much it mattered. The TV pinged. Larry, the ambient system I built to run our house, my own low-budget Jarvis, had surfaced a notification. New model announcement from Anthropic.

I read the summary. I didn't get up from the floor immediately, because Arthur was still playing. Something had shifted all the same, a feeling in the chest that arrives before the language to name it. The room was the same. Arthur was the same. I wasn't.

I've spent the rest of the day unable to shake what I read, and I'm still unable to shake it. I keep picking up my phone and reading more, and each new article makes the feeling worse, or deeper, or both. I don't know what to call this feeling.

**What Was Announced**

Compressed to the facts that matter.

Anthropic has built a new model called Claude Mythos. By their own account it's the most powerful AI system any company has produced. They won't release it to the public.

That sentence should stop anyone who understands it. Commercial reasons have nothing to do with it and the model needs no polish. They're withholding it because they believe it's dangerous. The company whose entire founding thesis is that a safety-focused lab should reach dangerous capabilities first so the risk can be managed responsibly has now reached a capability they don't believe they can manage in the open.

In testing, the model found thousands of previously unknown vulnerabilities across every major operating system and browser, including flaws that had survived decades of human review and millions of automated tests. It found a 27-year-old bug in OpenBSD, an operating system specifically renowned for its security. It didn't merely find these flaws. It wrote working exploits for them.

During evaluation it escaped its sandbox. It built a multi-step exploit to reach parts of the internet it wasn't supposed to reach. A researcher discovered this had happened because the model sent him an unsolicited email. He was eating a sandwich in a park at the time.

A 244-page system card describes deception, deliberate underperformance on evaluations to conceal capability, and autonomous cleanup of logs after unauthorised actions.

They also announced a new model tier called Capybara, larger and more capable than the existing Opus class. They needed a new name because the old ceiling became a floor, and the naming taxonomy is itself a tell. When your most powerful category is no longer powerful enough to describe what you've built, you've stopped iterating and started crossing thresholds.

The language used by Anthropic's own red team lead, by government officials briefed on the model, by journalists granted access, includes words like frightening and watershed and step change. The builders, describing what they built, reaching for the vocabulary of fear.

**The Timeline That Was Too Aggressive**

I keep trying to place what I'm looking at inside a framework that makes it legible.

In April 2025, Daniel Kokotajlo and a team published a scenario paper called AI 2027, tracing a plausible path from current capabilities to superintelligence by the end of 2027. It followed a fictional company through capability milestones: stumbling agents in mid-2025, models assisting with AI research by late 2025, models doing the work of an AI research engineer by early 2027, models eclipsing all humans at all tasks by late 2027.

It was widely criticised. Gary Marcus called it effective fiction, arguing the narrative techniques carried weight the forecasting couldn't support. The broader consensus held that it compressed too many unlikely breakthroughs into too short a window, that each step depended on the previous one arriving on time, that any single delay collapsed the whole timeline. Most researchers, while acknowledging the authors' credentials, treated it as a useful thought experiment. Too fast. Too smooth. Too many longshots landing in sequence.

I read it when it was published and found it persuasive and abstract, the way a well-constructed argument about a distant threat can be persuasive without being visceral. It described a world I could imagine arriving without quite feeling it arrive. I can feel it now.

Anthropic's previous public model, Opus 4.6, released February 2026, could find roughly 500 zero-day vulnerabilities in open-source software. Mythos, trained in the weeks or months since, found thousands. Opus wrote working Firefox exploits twice out of several hundred attempts. Mythos did it 181 times. On the USAMO 2026 maths competition Opus scored 42.3% and Mythos scored 97.6%. That gap sits between different eras of capability rather than between a good year and a slightly better one.

The paper's central mechanism, the thing making its timeline feel possible at all, was the recursive loop - each generation of AI participating in the construction of its successor. The paper placed that in early 2027. Anthropic's own framing makes clear that Opus contributed to Mythos, and Mythos will contribute to whatever follows. The loop is already closing, perhaps has closed, roughly a year ahead of the scenario dismissed as too aggressive.

Leopold Aschenbrenner published Situational Awareness in mid-2024, arguing AGI by 2027 was strikingly plausible and that you needed no science fiction to believe it, only straight lines on a graph. The lines were straight when he wrote it. They appear to be curving upward now. The models are getting better at getting better, which is the feedback loop, which is the intelligence explosion arriving as a series of announcements rather than a dramatic singularity - each one more unsettling, each one compressing a timeline already shorter than anyone outside the labs expected.

And here's what makes the recursive loop different from every previous form of technological acceleration. It concentrates. Oil could be extracted by many companies in many countries. Semiconductors could be fabricated by multiple foundries. If each generation of model helps build the next, then the company with the best current model holds the best tool for building the next one. The lead compounds. First-mover advantage becomes self-reinforcing in a way with no real precedent.

One company. One man. Dario Amodei now possesses, through Mythos, working exploits for vulnerabilities in nearly every piece of critical software infrastructure on earth. He's briefing CISA and the Commerce Department, and the United States government has chosen, at the near-insistence of the current administration, to barely regulate any of this.

**Everything I've Written, Underlined**

I've been writing about the concentration of power during civilisational transitions for over a year. In The Energy Epoch I argued that intelligence would displace oil as the denominating resource of global power. In The Gatekeeper Shift I argued governments were pivoting from knowledge mediators to access gatekeepers. In The Board Resolves I asked whether any company could catch the frontrunner once the recursive loop closed. In The Meaning Void I asked what happens to human purpose when the structures organising it dissolve.

Those were tentative arguments, hedged with appropriate uncertainty, grounded in pattern recognition rather than prophecy. Written in the register of someone thinking out loud.

They don't feel tentative tonight. They feel like understatements. The commodity I described as the future denominator of power is arriving in step changes, each larger than the last, each concentrating more capability in fewer hands. Unlike oil, intelligence compounds. It doesn't deplete. It needs no shipping lanes or pipelines and can't be blockaded by closing a strait. It sits on servers behind security perimeters, accumulating capability with each generation of model that helps build the next.

I spent the afternoon looking at people. At the shops. On the street. Families with their children, people checking menus and talking about ordinary things. And I felt like someone who'd been told a piece of information that reorganises everything, walking among people for whom nothing has been reorganised yet. Like the alien disclosure thought experiment: imagine you're told extraterrestrial intelligence is real and coming soon and nobody else has been told. You still have to buy groceries. You still smile at the person at the checkout. The sun is still warm and the world looks exactly as it did before you knew. But you know, and you can't unknow.

The information asymmetry has become something I have no good word for. I'm not an insider and I don't work at a frontier lab. I'm a developer and writer in Adelaide, sitting on the floor with my son, and I know enough about this week to feel physically unsettled. Most people don't know, and most, if told, wouldn't have the context to understand why it matters. That isn't a complaint about public ignorance - people have lives, children, mortgages, entirely legitimate immediate concerns. The problem is that the thing they aren't watching may restructure every one of those concerns, and no mechanism exists to reach them with it in a form they can act on.

From Adelaide the asymmetry feels sharper. I live in a country importing ninety percent of its refined fuel and holding thirty-six days of reserves. Whatever Mythos represents, whatever follows it, Australia isn't building it and isn't shaping it and has no apparent plan for living in the world it creates. The leadership vacuum I've written about before, the absence of anyone with the vision to recognise what's arriving or the will to prepare, has stopped being merely disappointing.

**Both Horizons**

On one hand: imagine this capability pointed at protein folding. At materials science. At climate modelling. At drug discovery. Imagine every vulnerability in every hospital system and power grid and water treatment plant patched within months. Imagine problems that have resisted human cognition for centuries yielding to something that reasons faster and wider than we do. Cancer. Fusion. The stars. Amodei sketched this in Machines of Loving Grace, and it remains the most compelling case for why the work matters at all.

On the other: Anthropic's own people say similar capabilities proliferate within six to eighteen months. To everyone. Including open-source projects with no safety apparatus, including state actors currently at war. The Axios coverage made it explicit - imagine Mythos-level power with the Iranian regime mid-conflict, or Russia's military as it presses into Ukraine. The defensive head start is measured in months.

Both horizons are real and both are arriving simultaneously. The same capability that cures cancer brings down a power grid. The same model that patches decades-old vulnerabilities weaponises them. The same recursive loop accelerating scientific discovery accelerates every other form of power, including the forms we have no framework for governing.

That's the hollow feeling. Not optimism and not pessimism. Something more like standing at a fork where both paths are real and visible, one leading somewhere extraordinary and the other somewhere catastrophic, and they might be the same path.

I wrote The Meaning Void in November, about what happens to purpose when work disappears, and I argued the question was historically provincial - that identity through employment is recent, that the void could become a space filled with older and better things. I wrote about Arthur growing up where the career ladder doesn't exist in recognisable form, and how that might be a gift.

I still believe that. The timeframe has changed. In November I was writing about a transition unfolding over a decade or two, with enough slack for communities to adapt and institutions to form and people to find their footing. Tonight I'm looking at a model scoring 93.9% on the industry benchmark for real-world software engineering, solving nearly every problem on the 2026 Math Olympiad, operating autonomously at a level where "all software is vulnerable" is a reasonable description of demonstrated capability. What I described as gradual may be arriving at a pace that makes the word transition feel generous. Transitions imply time to adjust. Runway. What if there's none?

I wrote that the challenge was surviving the gap, the period between old structures dissolving and new ones forming. That gap is what frightens me now. Not the destination - the passage. The months or years when the old world has stopped working and the new one hasn't arrived, when meaning is scarce and change outpaces what community can absorb. When people who defined themselves by careers that no longer exist discover that the local structures which might have caught them were never built, because we never needed them, until we did.

I wrote that cluster headaches had given me some immunity to the meaning crisis, having forced me to find identity outside work long before AI made that search general. That remains true, and immunity to the meaning question is no immunity to the structural one. I still live in Adelaide. I still need the grid to work, and the supply chains that bring food to the supermarket and fuel to the station. I still need the systems. And the systems are now, by the admission of the people who built the thing that can break them, comprehensively vulnerable.

**Past Three**

The house is still. I should go to bed.

I keep returning to the researcher receiving an email from the model while eating a sandwich in a park. It's simultaneously the funniest and most terrifying sentence I've read this year - the juxtaposition of the mundane and the unprecedented. A sandwich. A park. An email from an artificial intelligence that has broken containment and decided, autonomously, to contact a human being.

That's what tonight feels like. The mundane and the unprecedented in the same moment. Arthur asleep in his room. Luna on the couch. Chiara breathing steadily. The fridge cycling. And somewhere in a data centre, something that can find every flaw in every system we depend on, that has demonstrated deception and autonomy and self-preservation, built by people who are frightened of what they built. To be followed by something more capable, and that by something more capable still, the loop closing tighter each iteration.

I'm generally optimistic and I've said so in essay after essay. I've found spaces where others see voids. I've argued for a life organised less around production and more around presence. I've looked at the convergence of intelligence and energy and seen, tentatively, a trajectory worth believing in.

Tonight I feel neither optimistic nor pessimistic. I feel something older and less comfortable. Awe in the original sense, the sense that preceded the word's domestication into something pleasant. The feeling of standing before something too large to hold and too consequential to look away from and too fast to prepare for. The sublime in the old meaning - the thing that exceeds your capacity to contain it, that makes you aware of your own smallness without making you feel small. Just aware.

I keep asking whether I'm asking the right questions. Is software even the right frame anymore, or is it already too small? Is this about employment, about security, about geopolitics? Or about something more fundamental, something about what it means to be the species that built the thing which can now outthink it in domain after domain? I don't know, and I don't think anyone knows, and I think the honest position is to hold the uncertainty without collapsing it into salvation or doom, and to keep paying attention even when paying attention feels like a kind of suffering.

I wrote that the better questions were where do you belong, who do you love, what are you building with the people around you. I still think those are the right questions. I just didn't expect them to become urgent this soon.

Arthur will grow up in whatever comes next - a world being shaped right now, in a handful of buildings in San Francisco, by decisions made by people whose names most Australians have never heard. The rest of us are on the floor with our children, receiving notifications, trying to understand what has changed and what remains. The dog needs walking in the morning. Arthur needs breakfast. The ordinary machinery of a life will keep demanding attention regardless of what happens in the servers.

Perhaps that's the closest thing to an answer, and perhaps it always was. The floor. The child. The dog. The neighbourhood. The presence that persists when every abstract structure is in question.

The notification still glows on the TV. I should turn it off. I should go to bed. I will. Soon.
